title: Detect Cycles in 2D Grid
statement: `grid` is an `m x n` grid of lowercase letters. From a cell you may step to a neighbour above, below, left or right of it, but only when that neighbour holds the same letter. A **cycle** is a walk of 4 or more steps that begins and ends at the same cell, in which no step goes straight back to the cell visited on the step just before it (so `(1, 1) -> (1, 2) -> (1, 1)` does not count). Return `true` if the grid contains at least one cycle (necessarily made of one repeated letter), and `false` otherwise.
constraints: grid contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Treat every cell as a node and connect two side-by-side cells when they hold the same letter. A cycle in the grid is then just a cycle in this undirected graph (grid graphs have no triangles, so any cycle already has 4 or more steps). Explore each same-letter region with DFS while remembering which cell we came from. Each newly found cell is marked when it is first reached, so it is reached exactly once. If a cell sees a same-letter neighbour that is already marked and is not its own parent, there are two different routes to that neighbour, and together they form a cycle.

## Approach

1. Make a `visited` table and the four `directions`.
2. For every cell `(r, c)` not yet visited, mark it and push `[r, c, -1, -1]` (no parent) on a `stack`.
3. Pop a cell `(row, col)` with its parent `(fromRow, fromCol)` and look at its four neighbours.
4. Skip a neighbour that is outside the grid, holds a different letter, or is the parent.
5. If the remaining neighbour is already visited, return `true`; otherwise mark it and push it with `(row, col)` as its parent.
6. If every region is explored without that happening, return `false`.

## Example 1, step by step

The outer ring of `'a'` surrounds a `2 x 2` block of `'b'`. The search starts at `(0, 0)`, marking `(1, 0)` and `(0, 1)`. Following the stack it travels right along the top row, down the right column, left along the bottom row to `(3, 0)`, then up to `(2, 0)`. From `(2, 0)` the neighbour `(1, 0)` is an `'a'`, is not the parent `(3, 0)`, and was marked at the very start, so the ring is closed and the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n): every cell is pushed once and checks four neighbours.
- Space: O(m · n) for `visited` and the stack.

## Pitfalls

- Without the parent check, the step back to the cell you came from looks like a cycle of length 2.
- Mark a cell when it is pushed, so it enters the stack once with a single parent; only then does a marked neighbour that is not the parent reliably mean a second route.
- A recursive DFS can be thousands of calls deep on a large single-letter grid; an explicit stack avoids that.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rows`, `cols` | grid size |
| `visited` | whether each cell has been reached |
| `directions` | the four moves: down, up, right, left |
| `stack` | cells waiting to be explored, each with its parent |
| `row`, `col` | the cell being explored |
| `fromRow`, `fromCol` | the cell it was reached from (`-1` for a start) |
| `nextRow`, `nextCol` | the neighbour being checked |
